item.title: Perl Logging in 2026: Log::Log4perl vs Log::Dispatch vs Log::Any — Stop Guessing
item.description: Your Perl service has been running for nine years. It writes to three different log files because three different developers added logging in three different eras, one of them calls print STDERR inside a unless $quiet block, and nobody can turn on debug output for a single module without restarting everything. Every Perl shop has this file.

item.title: LWP::UserAgent vs Mojo::UserAgent vs HTTP::Tiny in 2026: Which Perl HTTP Client Should You Actually Use?
item.description: Perl ships an HTTP client in its standard library. That single fact has kept thousands of internal scripts dependency-free for a decade — and it has also trapped thousands of developers into a client that silently skips TLS verification when IO::Socket::SSL is missing. Meanwhile, the ecosystem’s heavyweight (LWP::UserAgent) is still at version 6.83 with a plugin tree going back to the 1990s, and Mojolicious ships a non-blocking client that most people never notice because they only think of it as a web framework.

item.title: Perl Testing in 2026: Test2::V0 vs Test::More vs Test::Deep — Which Stack Should You Run?
item.description: Perl has been shipping a test framework in core since 2001, which is both a gift and a trap. The gift is that prove and Test::More are there on every machine, with zero dependencies — you can test a script on a bare container image. The trap is that a decade of accumulated work sits behind a module most teams never migrate to: Test2, an event-based framework that fixes the architectural limits of the classic API, and which now powers CI suites that Test::More simply cannot express cleanly.

item.title: Raku Web Frameworks in 2026: Cro vs Bailador vs Humming-Bird (Honest Verdict)
item.description: Raku — the language formerly known as Perl 6 — has an actively maintained toolchain (Rakudo at 1,900 stars, MoarVM at 779, both committing within the last day) and a genuinely small web framework ecosystem. That combination is exactly why this comparison is useful: if you are considering Raku for a service, there are only three realistic answers, and two of them are not what you would pick for production in 2026.

item.title: Self-Hosted Web Development with Perl: Mojolicious vs Dancer2 vs Catalyst Framework Comparison (2026)
item.description: Despite decades of “Perl is dead” headlines, the Perl community continues to maintain and evolve several production-grade web frameworks. These frameworks power millions of sites and handle serious workloads — CPAN (the Comprehensive Perl Archive Network) remains one of the largest software repositories on the internet. If you’re building self-hosted web services and value stability, backwards compatibility, and battle-tested tooling, Perl’s web frameworks deserve a serious look.
